strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: predicting response times under changing external stimuli. Combining learned task representations with an evidence-accumulation process is a plausible approach, and Figure 1 makes the conceptual pipeline understandable.

The two-day behavioral study includes four randomized stimulus regimes and substantial repeated measurements from 36 analyzed participants. This provides useful task-specific evidence about practice and time-pressure effects.

Evaluation includes individual, group, pooled, and leave-one-participant-out settings, using both MAPE and correlation. The reported improvements over SVM and Pure DRL, together with lower training time on the same hardware, provide encouraging preliminary evidence.
weaknesses: Essential methodological details are missing. The supplied PDF references Appendices S2–S6 but does not include them. Consequently, the RL algorithm and reward definition, precise diffusion dynamics, mapping from SVM predictions to diffusion parameters, adaptive stimulus rule, and important training settings cannot be adequately assessed or reproduced. Statements promising future code and data availability do not resolve this omission.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution. Pure DRL removes both the diffusion model and frame-by-frame processing, confounding their effects. Missing comparisons include a fitted DDM with time-varying drift or boundaries and supervised sequential predictors receiving equivalent stimulus information. The suggestion that DDM is inherently retrospective rather than predictive is also overstated. These gaps weaken the claimed advantage over established cognitive and predictive approaches.

The claimed interpretation of frame-level cognitive mechanisms is unsupported by the observations. Trial-level choices and response times do not uniquely identify within-trial action trajectories; many trajectories can produce the same stopping time. Agreement with aggregate group trends therefore does not independently validate the inferred mechanisms. Nonzero 'time pressure effect' trajectories in the no-pressure group further suggest that actions can correct baseline prediction errors. Stimulus ablations and tests on independently varied stimulus time courses would help distinguish these explanations.

The incremental predictive gains are modest and their reliability is unclear. Figure 3 reports MAPE changing from 0.3034 to 0.2999 in pooled evaluation and from 0.3037 to 0.2905 in LOPO, approximately 1.2% and 4.3% relative improvements. No repeated-seed uncertainty or participant-level paired inference establishes robustness. The training-time comparison also lacks a clearly specified, comparable convergence criterion.

The evaluation pipeline leaves consequential ambiguities. It is unclear exactly which no-pressure observations train the baseline SVMs and whether normalization, SVM fitting, and model selection are performed entirely within each training fold, especially for LOPO. Thus, independence from held-out participants and the interpretation of the learned adjustment as a departure from untreated performance cannot be verified.

The behavioral interpretation exceeds the reported statistical evidence. Only the random-versus-none response-time comparison is reported significant; this does not establish that random stimulation is superior to every other regime. Nonsignificant accuracy differences likewise do not establish unchanged choice behavior. With only seven analyzed participants in the random group and unspecified criteria for excluding three extreme-outlier participants, uncertainty and sensitivity analyses are particularly important.
